alley-creature.title: 2:14 AM: A Creature in the Alley
alley-creature.description: A Gaussian-splat alley, relit in Blender, with a creature built entirely in Geometry Nodes crawling through it.

value.alt: The creature lunging down the alley in a grainy camcorder frame.
value.caption: A frame from the final cut.

content.value: This started as a one-day test. I wanted to see how far a Gaussian splat could go inside Blender: could I relight it, put something in it, and make the two feel like they share the same space? It turned into a short piece of found footage: a creature made entirely in Geometry Nodes, crawling through an alley at 2:14 in the morning.

value.text: A splat looks real from the right angle. The hard part is making anything else look like it belongs there.

content.value: 01. The Splat

The environment is Artillery Passage, a Gaussian splat I found on SuperSplat. It isn’t a mesh; it’s a cloud of soft, coloured points. From the right angle it looks like a photograph, but there’s no surface to light, nothing to cast a shadow on, and it falls apart as soon as the camera drifts too far.

value.caption: Moving through the raw splat. Push the camera too far and it breaks into points.

content.value: 02. Relighting
I relit the splat to pull it away from the flat daylight it came with, and added a simple collision plane underneath, with a post in the middle, so the creature had real surfaces to walk on and grab.

value.alt: The alley splat after relighting in Blender.
value.caption: The relit alley.

content.value: 03. A Creature Made of Nodes
Nothing in the creature is modelled by hand. The body, the legs and the feet all come from one node tree, so changing a single value changes the whole creature.

value.title: Body.
value.text: A soft central mass that every leg grows out of.

value.title: Legs.
value.text: Curves that reach out, bend and thicken into tar-like strands.

value.title: Feet.
value.text: Flat pads at each tip, so every leg looks stuck to whatever it lands on.

value.title: Material.
value.text: Dark and glossy, like wet tar or chewed gum, so it picks up the light of the alley.

items.alt: The creature in the Blender viewport, seen from the side.
items.label: Side

items.alt: The creature in the Blender viewport, legs spread across the alley walls.
items.label: Front

value.caption: The creature in the viewport, and a clay render of its movement before any material.

content.value: 04. Found Footage

The render took around 12 hours, and straight out of Blender the creature still looked too clean against the splat. I finished it in DaVinci Resolve: camera effects, grain, a green cast and a camcorder timestamp. The noise hides the soft edges of the splat, and the creature stops looking placed on top of the scene and starts looking recorded.

value.caption: The same shot, before and after DaVinci Resolve.

content.value: 05. Reflection

Splats are very good at looking real and not much good at anything else: light, contact and shadow all have to be built around them. Treating the final as found footage worked because it turns those weaknesses into part of the look.

diskfield.title: DiskField: Procedural Glass Disks
diskfield.description: A procedural Geometry Nodes system for a client project: a field of glass disks that turn, grow and glow orange as an effector passes through them.

value.alt: A diagonal line of glass disks, the ones nearest the effector turning orange.
value.caption: A frame from the line layout.

content.value: DiskField is a procedural Geometry Nodes system I built for a client project. It’s a field of thin glass disks that react to a moving effector: the disks closest to it turn, grow and glow orange, and the rest stay clear glass. Nothing is animated disk by disk. I move one effector, and the whole field responds.

value.text: One node tree, and the same idea becomes a line, a ring, a grid or any curve I draw.

content.value: 01. The Effect

Every disk measures its distance to the effector with Geometry Proximity. That one distance drives everything else: how far the disk turns, how big it gets and how much of the orange it takes on. A falloff keeps the change soft, so the colour travels through the field instead of switching on and off.

items.alt: The line layout in the Blender viewport, with the effector sphere among the disks.
items.label: In the viewport

value.caption: The effector passing along the line, and the same setup in the viewport.

content.value: 02. One System, Many Layouts
The layout is just a setting. The same node tree can place the disks along a line, around a ring, on a grid or along any path curve, and the effect behaves the same way in each.

items.alt: Disks arranged in a ring, the ones near the effector turned orange.
items.label: Ring

items.alt: A flat grid of small disks with an orange cluster around the effector.
items.label: Grid

items.alt: Disks following a curved path.
items.label: Curve

value.caption: Three layouts from the same setup.

value.alt: Rendered grid of glass disks with a soft orange cluster.
value.caption: The grid layout, rendered.

content.value: 03. Built to Be Changed
I built it as a set of controls rather than a single shot, so the look could change without rebuilding anything. Layout, shape and motion all sit on one modifier panel.

value.title: Layout.
value.text: Line, ring, grid or a path curve, with count, gap, jitter, seed and an option to stop disks overlapping.

value.title: Shape.
value.text: Radius, thickness, aspect, sides and bevel, each with its own randomness.

value.title: Effector.
value.text: An object that moves or orbits through the field, with a falloff that sets how far its influence reaches.

value.title: Look.
value.text: Lighting, backdrop and background text or image, so the same setup can sit in different compositions.

items.alt: The DiskField modifier panel with layout and shape controls.
items.label: Controls

items.alt: Part of the Geometry Nodes tree behind the setup.
items.label: Node tree

value.caption: The modifier panel, and part of the node tree behind it.

content.value: 04. Compositions
With the system in place, new compositions were a few settings away rather than a new scene each time.

items.alt: A wall of glass disks in rows with an orange cluster in the lower half.
items.label: Wall

items.alt: A soft, close render of the diagonal line.
items.label: Close up

value.caption: More looks from the same setup.

content.value: 05. Reflection
The time went into the system, not the shots. Once the proximity effect worked, every new layout, look or composition was a change of settings rather than a rebuild.

lithophane-lamp.title: Lithophane Lamp
lithophane-lamp.description: A photograph turned into a lithophane lamp: made first as a birthday gift, then turned into a standard workflow I now use to make them on demand.

value.alt: The lithophane lamp switched on, lying on a wooden floor.
value.caption: The finished lamp, switched on.

content.value: It started as a test for a birthday gift. I wanted to turn a photograph into something physical, so I converted it into a lithophane and designed a lamp around the print. The photograph is still there when the lamp is off, but it is the light passing through the print that brings out the detail. Once the first one worked, I turned the process into a standard workflow, and now I make them on demand.
01. From Photograph to Lithophane

A lithophane stores the tones of a photograph in the thickness of the material. Thinner areas let more light through and thicker areas let less through. There is no ink on the panel; the image comes from the geometry of the print itself.

items.alt: Unlit white portrait panel inside its frame.
items.label: Light off.

items.alt: The same portrait glowing in warm light.
items.label: Light on.

items.alt: A hand holding a lit lithophane lamp showing a different portrait.
items.label: Another portrait

value.caption: One lithophane with the light off and on, and another photograph made the same way.

content.value: 02. Building the Case

I modelled the enclosure in Blender around the dimensions of the lithophane. The body has grooves for the front panel, a separate cap and space inside for the lighting components. I kept the outside simple so the photograph remains the focus.

value.alt: Blender viewport of the enclosure with the portrait panel fitted.
value.caption: The lithophane fitted into the enclosure in Blender.

value.alt: Open enclosure showing the grooves and internal reflector disc.
value.caption: Inside the case, with the cap and front panel hidden.

content.value: 03. Spreading the Light

The light source is a small circular LED board. Lighting a lithophane directly from a small source can leave a bright spot in the middle and darker areas around it. I added a diffuser to scatter the light across the panel. The enclosure model also includes a reflector disc and space between the lighting components and the image.

value.alt: Circular LED board with several surface-mounted LEDs.
value.caption: The LED board used for the lamp.

content.value: 04. Printing and Assembly

I prepared the parts in Bambu Studio and printed them on my Bambu Lab A1 mini. The body, cap and internal disc were modelled as separate parts so they could be printed and assembled afterwards. The slicing setup shown here uses PLA, a 0.4 mm nozzle and a 0.2 mm layer height.

value.alt: Bambu Studio preview of the body, cap and circular disc on the print plate.
value.caption: The enclosure parts sliced in Bambu Studio.

content.value: 05. From One Gift to a Workflow

The first lamp was a one-off gift. After it worked, I standardised the process so the case, the light and the print settings stay the same, and only the photograph changes. Each new lamp no longer starts from scratch, which is what made it possible to start making them on demand.
06. The Finished Lamp

What I like about lithophanes is that the same object changes depending on how it is lit. With the light off, the photograph is a textured white surface. With the light on, the depth of the print becomes the contrast of the image. The case and diffuser are there to make that transition work as a lamp, rather than just a backlit print.

items.alt: Unlit lamp photographed from above at a slight angle.
items.label: The surface of the print in daylight.

items.alt: Illuminated portrait lamp against a dark background.
items.label: The portrait with the surrounding light reduced.

infrared-camera.title: Unseen: Infrared Camera
infrared-camera.description: A hand-built Raspberry Pi camera that shoots near-infrared photos and turns them into false colour. Work in progress.

value.alt: Near-infrared photo from the hand-built camera: magenta trees under a blue sky.
value.caption: First light. Leaves turn magenta while the sky stays blue.

value.text: Work in progress. This page covers the project up to Milestone 2. The camera shoots, but the false-colour pipeline, physical controls and body are still being built.

content.value: I’m building a camera that sees near-infrared light, the band just past visible red that classic infrared film like Kodak Aerochrome recorded. It isn’t a thermal camera. It captures reflected light and I process it into false colour.

I didn’t want it to be “a Raspberry Pi in a box”. It has a UI I designed in Figma, manual exposure on a real sensor, RAW capture, a rotary dial for control, an adjustable 550–750 nm filter, an IR flash and a power system I specced myself, all going into a 3D-printed body.

value.title: Status at Milestone 2
rows: Working: Pi 3 A+ with Camera Module 3 NoIR, JPEG and RAW
Phone control over Wi-Fi, live UI overlay, manual controls, gallery, settings
Frame stacking, false-colour pipeline, wiring the physical controls

content.value: First Results
I shot the same scene with my phone and with the camera. Anything that reflects a lot of infrared changes completely. Everything else barely moves.

value.alt: The scene shot on a phone camera.
value.caption: Phone camera, visible light

value.alt: The same scene from the NoIR camera.
value.caption: My camera, near-infrared

value.title: Leaves turn magenta.
value.text: Healthy foliage reflects a lot of infrared. With no IR-cut filter, that light lands in the red channel and pushes green toward magenta.

value.title: The sky stays blue.
value.text: Sky reflects little infrared, so it keeps its colour. That contrast is what makes IR photos look strange.

value.title: It depends on material, not colour.
value.text: Glass and dark cladding hardly change, and some yellow autumn leaves stay yellow.

content.value: This isn’t a controlled test. The two cameras differ in sensor, lens, framing and processing. Samples through 590 nm and 720 nm filters will be added later.
Choosing the Hardware

I set image quality by the Camera Module 3 NoIR (Sony IMX708, 12 MP, no IR-cut filter, autofocus, RAW). Its driver only really works on Raspberry Pi boards, so picking the sensor meant picking the Pi. After that, the question was which Pi.

rows: Smallest and cheapest, but out of stock and scalped
Other sensors were either 8 MP or missing colour tuning files
Bigger, hungrier, hotter. Wrong for a small camera
Runs the camera with no driver work, in stock, about €23. 512 MB RAM handled with swap

items.alt: Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+ next to the 2.8-inch ST7789 TFT display board.
items.label: Pi 3 A+ and the 2.8″ display

items.alt: A 37 mm variable infrared filter marked 550–750 nm.
items.label: 37 mm IR filter, 550–750 nm

value.caption: The core hardware, and the filter that sets which wavelengths reach the sensor.

content.value: Ideas I ruled out

value.title: Salvaging a DSLR sensor
value.text: Modern sensors use undocumented interfaces, and removing one usually destroys it.

value.title: Reusing an Android phone
value.text: The IR-cut filter can’t be removed cleanly, and cheap phones lock RAW access.

value.title: Fitting a Fujifilm lens
value.text: The module’s lens is fixed and the sensor is tiny, so the result would be blurry and heavily cropped.

content.value: Display

E-ink fit my first idea and uses almost no power, but it refreshes too slowly for a live viewfinder. A camera whose filter changes what the sensor sees needs one, so I went with a 2.8″ LCD. Preview and capture run on separate paths so processing never blocks framing.
Power

Power took more rounds than anything else. I developed on a 10,000 mAh power bank, but power banks are made to charge a phone and then sleep, and they cut out at low draw. Small banks couldn’t handle capture peaks, AA cells sag under load, and I ruled out salvaged vape cells for safety.
I chose a fixed 5 V, 3 A UPS board with one protected 18650 cell. I avoided boards with adjustable output, because one wrong setting would kill the Pi.
IR Flash

An infrared flash gives the sensor light the eye barely sees, which helps indoors, at night and through dark filters. I picked 850 nm over 940 nm because the sensor is much less sensitive at 940. Two small 3 W LED boards are switched by a logic-level MOSFET module, since the common IRF520 module can’t be driven properly from the Pi’s 3.3 V pins.
The Case

I modelled the case in Blender around the Pi, the camera module and the screen, and printed early versions to test the fit. Each print checks that the boards sit on their screw posts and that the ports and the lens line up with their openings.

items.alt: 3D-printed back plate with a raised camera mount and screw holes.
items.label: Back plate with camera mount

items.alt: 3D-printed panel with a round recess and a mount for the camera board.
items.label: Lens side

items.alt: Inside of a 3D-printed shell with screw posts and port cut-outs.
items.label: Shell with port cut-outs

items.alt: An earlier, simpler 3D-printed shell.
items.label: Earlier shell

value.caption: Early test prints of the case.

content.value: Software

All camera logic lives in one module, camera_core.py. The phone UI I use now and the physical screen and dial I’ll add later both call the same code. That let me build and test the whole interaction before the hardware arrived, and none of it gets thrown away.

layers.text: camera_core.py: preview, capture, exposure, RAW, settings

value.title: Controls, matched to the real sensor
rows: The sensor’s minimum gain rules out a true ISO 100
IR focuses at a different point than visible light

content.value: Interface Design
I designed the UI in Figma for a 320×240 screen, tested it in a browser simulator, then ran it as a live overlay on the real camera feed.

value.alt: Capture screen with exposure readouts.
value.caption: Capture: readouts and active-setting marker

value.alt: Capture screen with the manual focus scale.
value.caption: Manual focus scale

value.alt: Multi-frame stacking in progress.
value.caption: Frame stacking

value.alt: Multi-exposure, shot 1 of 2.
value.caption: Multi-exposure, shot 1 of 2

value.alt: Gallery screen.
value.caption: Gallery

value.alt: Settings screen.
value.caption: Settings

value.title: One setting at a time.
value.text: A marker shows what the dial controls. Pressing moves it from shutter to ISO to focus.

value.title: Corner brackets
value.text: frame the image without a heavy border and read instantly as a camera.

value.title: No filter readout.
value.text: The camera can’t sense which filter is on, so showing a value would be fake data.

content.value: After Figma

value.alt: The shoot overlay running on the camera.
value.caption: Shoot overlay, now in white

value.alt: The gallery in a dark theme.
value.caption: Gallery switched to dark

value: Figma exports text as shapes, so values couldn’t update. I moved layout and values into code and kept the icons as designed.
Black readouts vanished on dark scenes, so I switched them to white.
A white gallery was too bright on a small screen after framing a dim scene, so menus went dark.
Brightness became a 10-step bar you adjust with the dial, since pressing a button ten times doesn’t scale.

content.value: A Debugging Detour

An interrupted system update left about 50 packages broken, and every repair attempt killed my remote session. There were two causes. The 512 MB board was running out of memory, so I added swap by hand. And the first package to repair was the remote-access service I was connected through, so each attempt restarted it and cut me off. Running the repair as its own system service fixed it in one pass.
What’s Next

items: Double exposure with a ghost overlay

items: Process the RAW files with channel swaps and colour maps per filter
Add the 590 nm and 720 nm filter samples

value.title: Physical camera
items: Wire the screen, dial, buttons, flash and battery
Start on boot and finish the 3D-printed body

hiro-assistant.title: Hiro: Task Starting Assistant
hiro-assistant.description: A behavioural productivity assistant for the hardest part of any task: getting from meaning to start to actually starting.

value.alt: Hiro productivity assistant title

content.value: Hiro is a productivity assistant for the hardest part of work: starting it. Most tools focus on scheduling and task lists. Hiro focuses on the moment people get stuck, between meaning to do something and actually doing it.
It breaks the first step down, adjusts to how much energy you have, and nudges you toward a small first action, so starting takes less effort and keeping going gets easier.
Understanding Procrastination
Procrastination means postponing something that would benefit you if done today. This may include studying for exams, completing assignments, making phone calls, or finishing professional tasks.

value.alt: Procrastination

content.value: Research shows procrastination is not laziness but a coping mechanism used to temporarily escape unpleasant emotions such as anxiety, boredom, frustration, or self-doubt.
Neurological Explanation

At a neurological level, procrastination is a battle between two primary regions of the brain: the limbic system and the prefrontal cortex. The limbic system, often referred to as the emotional brain, prioritises immediate satisfaction and pleasure, seeking short-term fulfilment. The prefrontal cortex, in contrast, is responsible for more complex cognitive functions, including long-term planning, impulse control, and decision-making.
When tasks feel unpleasant or difficult, the limbic system prioritises immediate comfort over the logical reasoning of the prefrontal cortex, resulting in procrastination.
Additional Causes of Procrastination

value: Many people believe motivation must come before action, when in reality action often creates motivation.
Fear of failure is a major cause of task avoidance.
Perfectionists delay tasks because they believe everything must be done perfectly.
Self-criticism and unrealistic expectations reinforce avoidance behaviour.
Frequent 'should' statements create guilt and resentment, leading to further procrastination.

content.value: Existing Productivity Approaches
One traditional approach to overcoming procrastination is SMART goal setting.

value: Define clear and precise study goals
Track progress using checklists or measurable outputs
Break the goal into smaller concrete achievable steps

value.alt: SMART

content.value: Other behavioural techniques include establishing a routine, preparing tasks for the next study session, and rewarding yourself after completing goals.
User Research
To understand real behaviour patterns, I conducted a Google survey targeting students, young adults, and early professionals.

value: Primary users: students, young professionals, early career workers
Digital-native behaviour with heavy smartphone usage
People juggle study, work, and personal responsibilities

content.value: Behavioural Insights
The research indicates that people are not lazy; they are context-sensitive starters.
What Users Do Instead
Users rarely remain inactive. Instead they switch to easier tasks that provide immediate psychological rewards.
Emotional State After Procrastinating
Users already experience psychological cost after procrastinating. Therefore guilt-based design approaches are ineffective.
Core UX Problem Statement

Young adults delay tasks not because of lack of motivation, but because of low energy, unclear starting points, and distant deadlines. This leads to task switching toward easier activities and increased stress.
User Personas
Rick Austin, The Overloaded Student (20)

value: Delays tasks when they feel complex
Switches to social media when unsure how to begin
Behavioural Insight: Rick avoids the unclear beginning of large tasks.
Quote: 'I'll start after one reel… maybe after this one.'
Design Need: Automatic task breakdown and quick first action.

content.value: Riya Jerald, Independent Planner (38)

value: Delays work when urgency feels low
Design Need: Visual deadline compression and progress visibility.

content.value: Rahul Dev, Balancing Professional (29)

value: Struggles with mental fatigue after work
Behavioural Insight: Rahul engages in productive procrastination.

content.value: User Journey Map: The Delay Loop

value: I'll do it later when I feel ready.
Comfortable → Guilty
Now I HAVE to do it.

content.value: Critical observation: the highest friction point occurs between intention and starting.
Experience Breakdown: Cognitive States
Theoretical Framework: Temporal Motivation Theory

Temporal Motivation Theory (TMT) explains procrastination as a decision-making process in which people choose the activity with the highest perceived motivational value at a given moment. Tasks with immediate rewards are often prioritised over tasks with delayed benefits, even if the long-term outcome is more important.
The theory describes motivation using the following formula:
Each variable represents a psychological factor that influences whether a person starts or delays a task.

value.title: Expectancy
value.description: Confidence in successfully completing the task

value.title: Value
value.description: How rewarding or enjoyable the task feels

value.title: Sensitivity to Delay
value.description: Preference for immediate rewards over delayed benefits

value.title: Time Delay
value.description: The time until the reward or outcome is received

content.value: Design Implications

value: Expectancy: Increase confidence by breaking large tasks into smaller steps.
Value: Increase perceived reward through micro-progress and feedback.
Sensitivity to Delay: Reduce impulsive switching by providing quick start actions.
Time Delay: Reduce perceived delay through timeline compression and intermediate checkpoints.

content.value: Motivation increases when expectancy and value increase while delay decreases.
Product Concept - Hiro
I kept the concept narrow on purpose. Hiro doesn't plan your week or manage your tasks. It only deals with the moment you get stuck between meaning to start and starting.

The system helps users begin tasks by automatically breaking them into manageable steps, suggesting actions based on the user’s current energy level, and enabling optional co-working sessions that provide light social accountability.
Why the name Hiro?
The name Hiro comes from a conceptual blend of:

value: Hermes the messenger and guide who helps movement and transition.
Kairos the greek diety representing the concept of the right time

content.value: Together, the name reflects the purpose of the system: Helping users recognise and act in the right moment to begin work.
The name also phonetically resembles “Hero,” reinforcing the idea that users take small steps toward overcoming procrastination.
Behavioral Model: The Procrastination Loop
User behaviour often follows a predictable procrastination loop driven by uncertainty, low urgency, and immediate distractions.
This cycle shows that the real problem is not completing tasks but starting them.
Hiro Intervention Model
Hiro interrupts the procrastination loop before avoidance begins by reducing cognitive friction and helping users take the first action.
Information Architecture

value: Tasks: Active tasks and task breakdown
Energy Mode: Current energy level selection

content.value: Visual Development

I called Hiro’s design system The Digital Sanctuary. Most productivity tools feel rigid and demanding, like a digital clipboard. I wanted Hiro to feel calmer, closer to a quiet library than a to-do list.

value.alt: Hiro visual layout and design system overview

content.value: Colour: Tonal Architecture
The palette is a dialogue between Sage (primary), Muted Blue (secondary), and Warm Cream (background). Colour is used to make the app feel calm, not to raise alarms.

value: No 1px lines: sections are separated by background colour only

content.value: Typography

value: 3.5rem: welcome states, lots of open space

content.value: Large headlines use tight tracking (−0.02em) to feel premium. Body copy stays at body-md to ensure the interface never feels dense.
Screen Flow
Instead of overwhelming users with large tasks, Hiro always presents a single, achievable starting action.
System 1 - Intelligent Task Breakdown

value: Breaks large tasks into smaller actions

value.alt: Task upload screen 1
Task upload screen 2
Task upload screen 3

content.value: Users begin by adding a task to Hiro by entering its name and deadline. Rather than presenting the full scope of the work, the system immediately breaks it down into smaller, manageable steps using the Gemini API.

Gemini analyses the task and generates a structured breakdown, splitting the work into milestones scheduled across the available time before the deadline, with built-in buffer time to reduce last-minute pressure.

value.alt: Task breakdown screen 1
Task breakdown screen 2

content.value: System 2 - Energy Based Task Assignment

Once the task is broken down, Hiro doesn't hand the user a flat to-do list. Instead, it surfaces different suggested steps depending on the user's current energy level, so someone running low can still get something done without feeling buried.

value.alt: Energy level 1
Energy level 2
Energy level 3

content.value: Snooze mode - Intentional Pause

Snooze Mode allows users to temporarily pause tasks, reminders, and notifications when they need time to rest or step away. Hiro doesn't push you to stay productive all the time. Resting is part of keeping focus.

Users can choose predefined durations or create custom schedules, so a break is a decision, not a way of avoiding the task. All progress is preserved, and tasks are gently reintroduced once the snooze period ends.
This feature prevents burnout while maintaining a clear path back to action, supporting a healthier and more sustainable productivity cycle.

value.alt: Snooze screen 1
Snooze screen 2

content.value: Core Product Capabilities
Example Scenario
A student enters the task 'Write essay, due in 7 days'. Hiro automatically creates milestones and suggests today's first action: Find three research sources (10 minutes).
Break Reminder

value.alt: Break Reminder screen 1
Break Reminder screen 2

content.value: Most productivity apps remind users to start a task very often. But users already feel pressure to start. Adding more start-reminders increases anxiety rather than motivation.

value: Suggests breaks at the right moment

content.value: This avoids notification fatigue. Instead of pushing users to begin, Hiro steps back once work has started. It stays quiet during focus and only suggests breaks when they help.
Conclusion

Working on Hiro changed how I see procrastination. It isn't a scheduling problem, so a stricter planner won't fix it. The design had to focus on the moment of starting, and make the first step small and clear enough to take.

city-in-hand.title: City in Hand: 3D-Printed Dublin
city-in-hand.description: Turning a captured 3D map of Dublin into a physical, 3D-printed object, reducing 10,000 fragmented meshes to one printable model.

value.alt: The finished 3D-printed relief map of central Dublin.
value.caption: The finished model: a printable relief map of central Dublin, assembled from five plates.

content.value: City in Hand is a personal R&D project: take a detailed 3D map of a city and turn it into an object you can hold. What began as “export the map, print it” became a deep dive into graphics capture, mesh repair, and the gap between geometry that renders on a screen and geometry that survives in the physical world.

value.text: The file was only a few megabytes. What froze Blender was the ten thousand separate objects inside it.

content.value: The Goal

The source geometry was captured frame-by-frame from a real-time 3D map using RenderDoc, a graphics debugger that intercepts what an application sends to the GPU. The aim was purely technical and non-commercial: learn the capture-to-physical pipeline end to end and print the city I live in.

value.alt: Model in Blender.
value.caption: A captured frame in Blender, while the model is being optimized.

content.value: 01. Ten Thousand Fragments
The capture produced roughly 10,000 individual mesh files, with every building, road tile and prop saved as its own object. It was only a few megabytes on disk, but Blender froze on import.

I assumed the file was too big, but size wasn’t the issue. Blender was doing ten thousand separate imports and rebuilding its dependency graph each time. From then on, my goal was to cut the number of objects, not the file size.
02. A Custom Merge Pipeline
Standard tools failed one after another, so I wrote a script to take control. Three problems had to be solved:

value.title: Missing textures.
value.text: Absent files crashed every read, so I patched the file-read layer to return empty data so geometry loaded regardless.

value.title: Changed API.
value.text: The merge library’s old method had been removed, so I switched to the current one.

value.title: Buffer limit.
value.text: The format allows one data buffer; merging produced 10,000, so I collapsed them into one before writing.

content.value: Result: 10,007 files merged, zero failures, compressed from ~380 MB to 70 MB. It still froze.
03. Compression Isn’t Consolidation

The compressed file still held nearly 10,000 meshes. It was smaller, but no simpler. The standard “join” also refused to weld them, because each mesh’s position was baked into its vertices rather than stored as a transform.

The fix was to bypass the scene structure entirely: decompress, read the raw vertices from every mesh, and concatenate them into one. The result was 1 mesh with 7.5M vertices and 5.5M faces. At 18 MB, it opened instantly.

value.alt: The welded single-mesh city map open in Blender.
value.caption: All ~10,000 fragments welded into one mesh.

content.value: 04. Too Detailed to Print

Millions of faces is more than a slicer wants, but naive simplification destroys what makes a city readable: sharp building edges. Voxel Remesh works well for organic forms, but it blurred walls and spires into blobs. Planar Decimate collapsed flat surfaces while keeping corners crisp.

items.title: Merge by Distance
items.description: Removed duplicate vertices with no visual change.

items.title: Decimate: Planar
items.description: Simplified flat surfaces, kept building edges sharp.

items.title: Decimate: Collapse
items.description: Handled organic tree geometry planar mode couldn’t touch.

items.title: Print-scale thinking
items.description: Detail finer than a 0.4 mm nozzle won’t print, so there’s no point keeping it.

content.value: 05. Watertight for the Physical World

Screen geometry only needs to look right. Printed geometry must be a closed solid. The mesh had hundreds of thousands of open edges and hundreds of disconnected shells. One-click “make manifold” tools mangled detail, so the fix was a sequence: clean up first, reduce, then run a patch-based repair that fixes holes without softening detail.
06. Repair First, Then Cut
The map was larger than the print bed. Cutting a broken mesh just produces several broken pieces; cutting a clean solid produces clean, closed pieces. I added interlocking connectors at the seams.
07. The Print That Wouldn’t Stick

Large flat prints give cooling corners maximum leverage to peel. PLA barely warps, so the problem was adhesion, not temperature. Washing the plate with soap and water made the biggest difference. I also widened the brim, re-levelled the bed and turned off first-layer cooling.

value.alt: The city map printing on a Bambu A1 mini with a wide brim.
value.caption: Printing cleanly after the adhesion fixes.

content.value: The Result
3D Map: Dublin City is published free on MakerWorld. Print profile: 0.12 mm layers · 2 walls · 15% infill · tuned for the Bambu A1 mini.

value.alt: The finished Dublin city map print.
Close-up detail of the printed Dublin buildings.

content.value: What I Took Away

value.title: Diagnose the real bottleneck
value.text: The number of objects mattered, not the file size.

value.title: Know when to leave the toolbox
value.text: When every standard tool failed the same way, reading the geometry directly solved it.

value.title: Rendering ≠ manufacturing
value.text: Geometry that looks solid on screen can be full of holes once it must become real.

value.title: Order of operations matters
value.text: Reduce before repair, repair before cut.

dub-transit.title: Dub.Transit: Dublin Public Transport App
dub-transit.description: A real-time transit application that simplifies navigating Dublin’s transport network with simple route search, live bus tracking, service alerts, weather, and an AI assistant for planning trips.

value.alt: The dub.transit wordmark over a map of central Dublin

content.value: Dub.Transit is a mobile application built to unify Dublin’s fragmented public transport information into one clear, simple app.
The app combines:

value:
Route Search & Stop Lookup
Find any route or stop across the network.

Live Network Map
Real-time visuals with simulated tracking.

Service Alerts
Live updates for events, delays, and accidents.

AI Journey Planning
Smart assistance powered by Gemini.

Weather-Aware Guidance
Travel advice based on live forecast.

content.value: Problem & Opportunity
Dublin’s transport experience is often fragmented:
User Research Findings

value: -Commuters want quick and simple route lookup (bus numbers, origins/destinations).
-Dublin residents rely on Google Maps, but hate its delay unpredictability.

value.alt: Traffic control during St Patrick's day

content.value: Opportunity
Create a single, friendly, modern app that integrates routing, AI guidance, alerts, weather, and live tracking together.
Design Process & UX Approach
User Requirements
Through informal interviews with students, workers, and migrants in Dublin, I identified key priorities:

value: “Just show me where the bus is.”
“I don’t want to figure out inbound/outbound.”
“I just want a clean app that works.”
“Weather screws up my commute, tell me beforehand.”

content.value: These insights shaped the core flows.

I chose a dark, modern UI with a yellow similar to the Dublin bus color (#E3CD00) as the primary accent.

value.alt: Colorscheme for the app

content.value: Reasons:
Prototyping & Iteration
I iterated through several cycles:

value: Redesigned direction labels from Inbound/Outbound → A → B / B → A
Rebuilt the map for readability and smooth marker animation
Optimised the AI planner’s information density (steps, ETA, weather)
Refined empty states and loading behaviours to reduce user stress
Enhanced the weather integration after feedback (“show arrival weather too”)

content.value: AI-Assisted Prototyping Process
This prototype heavily used AI tools during iteration:

value: Google AI Studio: initial drafts of features & logic
DeepSeek: refining data structures, simulation logic, and route handling
ChatGPT: final refinements, debugging, API integration, UX adjustments

value.alt: Usage of Google AI Studio for the development

content.value: AI helped speed up prototyping, letting me focus on design and experience rather than spending too much time on development.
Live Prototype
To make Dub.Transit accessible directly from the browser, I created a web-based preview of the app. This allows the viewers to interact with the interface without installing the Android app.
https://dublintransporttracker.netlify.app

value: You can also open the app in a new tab to explore it fully.

content.value: The current version preserves the overall UX, typography, and component layout so viewers can understand the design system.
Advanced Features
Weather Integration

Using Open-Meteo, the app fetches: Current temperature, Feels-like, Rain probability, Wind, Weather at arrival time, for journey planning This allows the AI to adjust trip suggestions (e.g., “Expect rain when you arrive at St. Stephen’s Green”).

value.alt: Weather at your location and destination

content.value: Gemini AI Journey Assistant
A central highlight of the project.

The assistant: Reads user’s start + destination, Checks possible transport modes, Considers weather conditions, Provides a human-readable plan, Gives suggestions (“Leave 10 minutes early, traffic is heavy near Drumcondra”).
Gemini acts as the smart layer on top of the transit data.

value.alt: Step-by-step navigation

content.value: Crowdsourced Real-Time Tracking (Future Feature)
The next big piece for Dub.Transit is community-powered bus tracking, to fill the gaps in Dublin's existing live data.
Why Crowdsourcing?
GTFS-Realtime (GTFS-R) feeds are:

value: out of scope for a prototype project

content.value: Although GTFS-Realtime is a standard, its accuracy in Dublin varies, and buses frequently jump, freeze, or move in the wrong direction, which is exactly what I experienced while testing.
Crowdsourcing solves this by decentralizing the live tracking system, similar to how Waze collects real-world traffic data from its drivers.
How the Crowdsourced System Works?
With user consent, the app would:

value: Detect when a passenger is inside a bus (based on movement patterns + manual confirmation).
Upload minimal, anonymous data such as:
Combine data from multiple passengers on the same route.
Smooth and interpolate positions on the backend to produce a highly accurate, real-time view.

content.value: Privacy-Preserving Design

value: No background tracking unless explicitly enabled
Data expires and is deleted automatically after a few minutes
Users opt-in on a per-trip basis

content.value: Limitations & Technical Challenges
Crowdsourcing isn’t magic, it introduces a new set of challenges:

value: Requires a critical mass of active users

content.value: --(early versions may have sparse tracking)

value: Data quality varies

content.value: --(e.g., inaccurate GPS, people on the wrong bus)

value: Requires server-side smoothing

content.value: --(Kalman filtering, interpolation, direction correction)

value: Detecting whether a user is genuinely on a bus

content.value: --(signal patterns, speed, or manual confirmation)

value: User outreach is essential

content.value: --The quality of tracking depends directly on the number of participants.
I present these limitations openly as part of the project’s honest, real-world constraints.
Prototype Status & Future Improvements
The current version of Dub.Transit is a functional prototype, with:

value: fully working AI-powered journey planner (Gemini API)
Working route search, stop lookup, and route shapes
Simulated live buses moving along real route geometry
Cross-platform mobile UI built in React Native

content.value: What’s next?
Here’s the roadmap for turning this into a full production app:
Final Thoughts
Dub.Transit started as a way to put Dublin's scattered transport information in one app. Along the way it pulled in UX, visual design, mobile development, map logic and AI.

The process taught me that designing for transit is really designing for people: their routines, their worries, their unpredictability, and the clarity they need when something goes wrong. Gemini is already in the app, and crowdsourced bus positions are next. The aim stays simple: make getting around Dublin a bit easier, and fairer.
“A developed country is not a place where the poor have cars. It's where the rich use public transportation.”
content.author: Gustavo Petro (Former Mayor of Bogotá, Colombia)

city-beneaththesurface.title: City: Beneath the Surface
city-beneaththesurface.description: An interactive data visualization and public installation that reveals the invisible labor sustaining cities by turning public sentiment into visuals that move and change.

value.alt: Title card

content.value: “No work is insignificant. All labor that uplifts humanity has dignity and importance and should be undertaken with painstaking excellence.”
content.author: Martin Luther King Jr.

content.value: Project Overview

City: Beneath the Surface is an interactive installation about care-based labor in cities. It shows the people who keep a city running (bus drivers, waste collectors, maintenance crews and others) as bubble networks that grow and shift with public sentiment and context data.

It's meant for everyday public spaces like bus stops and train stations, so people come across this work where it actually happens.
Context & Motivation

value: Growing up in India, I observed cultural stigma toward manual and public-facing labor, often framed as “low-status” work.
In contrast, while studying in Dublin, I noticed greater respect and infrastructural support for these workers, yet still a lack of emotional recognition.
This project became both a personal reconciliation and a design intervention, aiming to shift public narratives by making invisible labor visible

value.alt: Photograph of a street in India with visible waste, illustrating the project's personal motivation.

content.value: “YOU WILL END UP PICKING TRASH, IF YOU DON'T STUDY WELL”
content.author: A Random Teacher from My School

content.value: Problem Statement

Despite being essential, care-based workers remain socially undervalued. Public frustration with systemic failures is often misdirected toward visible figures like drivers or cleaners, reinforcing stigma and invisibility
Research Question
How might contextual data visualization be used to reframe public narratives surrounding care-based labor?

value.alt: A person interacting with the 'City, Beneath the Surface' installation on a large public screen.

content.value: Objectives

value: Expose the hidden tiers of labor that sustain the city.
Collect and visualize sentiment data around urban workers.
Build a responsive installation that shifts based on public interaction.
Challenge stigma by connecting emotions, data, and design.

content.value: Design Concept

value.alt: Diagram illustrating the project's design concept: data input leads to interactive visualization and an AR layer.

value: Dynamic Bubbles: Each sector of urban labor (waste, water, transport, construction, electrical, sanitation, emergency, etc.) is represented as a parent bubble. Roles and sub-roles emerge around it, creating a living hierarchy of workers.
Network Visualization: The installation shows how different sectors connect and interdepend to keep the city functioning, emphasizing systemic collaboration rather than isolated roles.
Public Interaction: Users can tap or click bubbles to reveal details about roles, responsibilities, and worker counts within each sector.

Augmented Reality Layer: In the mobile app, the AR view links the virtual system to real-world objects. For example, pointing at a bus, trash can, or streetlight reveals the associated bubble, its sector, and data about the number of workers behind it.
Atmosphere: Idle animations and floating motion give the system a “living” quality, symbolizing the ongoing, often unnoticed work beneath the city.

content.value: Theoretical Frameworks

value: Everyday Life and Cultural Theory (Ben Highmore) → Centers ordinary, undervalued labor as culturally significant.

value.alt: Slide explaining the theoretical framework of 'Everyday Life and Cultural Theory by Ben Highmore'.

value: Maintenance and Care (Shannon Mattern) → Frames maintenance as essential, emotional, and infrastructural labor.

value.alt: Slide explaining the theoretical framework of 'Maintenance and Care by Shannon Mattern'.

value: Convergence Culture (Henry Jenkins) → Informs how public narratives and digital participation shape collective meaning.

value.alt: Slide explaining the theoretical framework of 'Convergence Culture by Henry Jenkins'.

content.value: These ideas shaped the main goal: make invisible work visible, and show workers as part of the city's culture, not only as the jobs they do.
Tools & Development

value: Early Prototyping: Initial concepts tested in p5.js to explore visual states and interaction ideas. Some other concepts were also explored, using 3D models and map data of the city.

content.value: Prototype using map data and 3D models in blender

value.alt: Early 3D prototype in Blender: a city map with data points

content.value: Second Prototype using p5.js

value.alt: Screenshot of a p5.js prototype with colorful circular data points on a dark background.

content.value: Built as a web-based interactive installation with an accompanying mobile AR app.

value: Development Workflow: Iteratively coded using ChatGPT, Claude.ai, and Google AI Studio, with final refinements and debugging done manually.

value.alt: Screenshot of code being generated using an AI tool, illustrating the project's development workflow.

value: Delivery Platforms: Public Installation → large screen or projection in transit hubs. Mobile Application → includes Hierarchy View and AR View linking bubbles to real-world city objects.

content.value: User Journey - Storyboard

value.alt: Storyboard: from noticing the installation to using it

content.value: Final Output

value: Mobile AR App UI Prototypes: Extends the installation into everyday life, letting users scan familiar city objects to uncover the workers and systems behind them.

value.alt: AR app: hierarchy view and camera view

value: Interactive Visualization: A responsive bubble system representing the city’s essential workers.

value.title: City, Beneath the Surface - Live Installation

content.value: You can also open the installation in a new tab to explore it fully.

value: Exhibition Setup: Designed for public spaces where passersby can engage with the installation and explore hidden labor systems.
Message: Cities depend on labor most people never see. This project makes that labor visible as an interactive network.

content.value: Reflection
This project taught me a few things:

value: Interactive visualization makes complex labor systems easier to approach, and puts people back into the numbers.
Real datasets, not only sentiment, keep the story grounded, and it can still feel poetic.
The potential and limits of AI-assisted coding as a design partner, and the importance of taking creative control in the final refinements.
Clarity and exploration pull against each other. The piece has to make sense to someone walking past, and still hold up for institutions and stakeholders.

value.alt: Final exhibition shot of the data visualization glowing on a screen in a dark room.

content.value: Project Overview
Theyyam Threads turns Kerala's Theyyam art form into T-shirt designs. I wanted to keep the look and the meaning of the ritual, and put it on something people actually wear.

value.alt: A person wearing the Theyyam t-shirt, looking away from the camera in a stylish pose.

content.value: Sketch was made as a joint effort of me and my friend Adithya. We tried to explore several forms based on our references and came up with the idea of just the facial expression of Theyyam. Some sparks were also added later in front to show the intense artform.

content.value: Later we decided to go with a  monochrome approach, showing just the black and white elements.

Working on this meant reading into where Theyyam comes from and what it stands for, not just how it looks. The shirts became a small way to carry that tradition to people who might never see a performance.
